source_read: PDF (version of record), International Journal of Drug Policy 143 (2025) 104867, pp. 1-10 (all pages read in a pdftotext extraction; Tables 1-4 checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi, Table 4 also at 300 dpi; Fig. 1 read on the rendered page, Fig. 2 at 300 dpi). For the two claims that also cite other sources, only the Gelberg parts were checked.

claims.overstatement: Gelberg part. Not supported: 'the study ... measures neither harm nor overdose'. The Stay Safe Study collected overdose in the past 30 days at baseline, used here as a covariate (p. 2, Surveys; p. 3, Statistical analyses), and the claim set elsewhere cites the same study's companion paper (Vickers-Smith et al., 2025, cited here on p. 3) for self-reported overdoses during the 28 days. Accurate: 'this paper analyses neither harm nor overdose'. Needs a qualifier: 'largest when the drugs tested included illicit benzodiazepines (odds ratio 19.9)' repeats the printed odds ratio, but the benzodiazepine row's own modelled probabilities in Table 4 imply an odds ratio of about 3.6 to 5.3 (editors' calculation), smaller than the stimulants-only row (about 8.5 to 10.4, printed 10.04); the other rows reproduce their printed ratios approximately. The benzodiazepine estimates are also very imprecise (using more after a negative result 0.657, 95% CI 0.091 to 0.973), the number of people or tests per subgroup is not printed, and the authors call every estimate other than the primary any-change association descriptive and unadjusted for multiple comparisons (pp. 3, 5). Small wording points: the item is 'used near someone who had naloxone', not 'keeping naloxone nearby' (Table 3); the odds ratio is a proportional-odds ratio for a smaller rather than larger amount (it applies to less against same or more and to same or less against more), not only 'less rather than the same or more'.
claims.note: All Gelberg numbers check against Tables 2-4 on the rendered pages (Table 4 at 300 dpi): 541 analysed, May-December 2023, Kentucky, New York and Ohio; OR 4.373 (3.448-5.545) overall, 19.918 (8.573-46.273) benzodiazepines, 10.041 stimulants only, 4.207 opioids and stimulants, 2.176 opioids only, 2.110 other or unknown; using more after a negative result 0.657 (benzodiazepines), 0.531 (stimulants only), 0.373 (opioids only), 0.225 (overall); after a positive result overall 0.090 less or none, 0.847 same, 0.063 more. Implied odds ratios from Table 4's probabilities (editors' calculation; less or none against same or more / less, none or same against more): overall 4.20 / 4.32; opioids only 2.18 / 2.10; stimulants only 10.35 / 8.46; opioids and stimulants 3.94 / 3.73; benzodiazepines 3.64 / 5.28; other 2.03 / 2.01. The abstract's 'fold reductions' are these odds ratios (p. 1), as the claim says; the abstract also merges opioids alone and other drugs as '2-fold ... OR=2.11', which is the other-drugs ratio (opioids alone 2.18). No comparison with people not offered strips: all were recruited from programmes distributing strips and the study gave none (p. 2).

anchors.locator: Methods › Study design, 1st paragraph; Participants; Surveys, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Observational cohort, May to December 2023, recruited from community harm-reduction programmes (including syringe services) actively distributing strips in Kentucky, New York and Ohio; the study gave no strips; adults reporting past-30-day use of listed drugs; baseline survey included overdose in the prior 30 days.
Four weekly surveys: for each day of drug use, drugs used, strip use and results for up to two tests a day, then any of 12 listed behaviour changes made because of the result, or none.
1,405 screened, 1,201 eligible, 1,156 enrolled, 732 completed baseline and at least two weekly surveys and used drugs, 541 (73.9%) used strips at least once and form the analysis sample.

GEE models adjusted for state, age, race, ethnicity, sex, education, employment, prior strip instruction, past-30-day overdose and daily time-varying covariates; amount used modelled as a proportional-odds (cumulative logit) outcome, with modification by drug type tested; only the any-change association was the primary hypothesis, no adjustment for multiple comparisons, other p-values 'purely descriptive'.

Odds ratio of a reduction in amount, positive against negative result: overall 4.373 (3.448-5.545); illicit opioids only 2.176 (1.442-3.283); stimulants only 10.041 (6.494-15.526); opioids and stimulants 4.207 (2.742-6.454); illicit benzodiazepines 19.918 (8.573-46.273); other or unknown 2.110 (1.136-3.922). Using more after a negative result: 0.225 overall, 0.373 opioids only, 0.531 stimulants only, 0.546 opioids and stimulants, 0.657 (0.091-0.973) benzodiazepines; after a positive result 0.063 overall, 0.266 (0.038-0.689) benzodiazepines.

anchors.locator: Table 4, benzodiazepine row (editors' calculation) and footnote [1]
anchors.extracted: The benzodiazepine row's probabilities (positive 0.032 / 0.701 / 0.266; negative 0.009 / 0.334 / 0.657) imply odds ratios of about 3.6 and 5.3 at the two cut-points, not 19.9; other rows reproduce within about 20%. Footnote [1] announces the number of participants per model, but no column gives it.

anchors.locator: Table 3, rows 'took turns', 'used near someone who had naloxone', 'used less'
anchors.extracted: Positive against negative: took turns 0.24 against 0.19 (ratio 1.29, 1.05-1.59); used near someone with naloxone 0.23 against 0.15 (1.54, 1.16-2.05); used less 0.11 against 0.02 (5.54, 2.52-12.19).

Abstract: 'four-fold reduction' (OR 4.37), '20-fold reduction' for benzodiazepines (OR 19.92), '2-fold reduction' for opioids or other drugs (OR 2.11); concludes that strips help people immediately reduce risk, including the amount used.

Self-reported results and behaviour (recall, social desirability); unknown whether negatives reflect improper use; associations, not causal; unmeasured confounding; clients of harm-reduction services in three states; false positives and negatives not examined.

claims.overstatement: None material for the Gelberg part. Two precisions: the four-fold figure is a proportional-odds ratio for reporting a smaller rather than a larger amount (it applies equally to less against same or more and to same or less against more; Table 4 note [2]), so 'an odds ratio for reporting less rather than the same or more' is half the description; in absolute terms most of the contrast is fewer reports of using more (6 against 23 in 100) rather than more reports of using less (9 against 2). And behaviour was asked for up to two tests a day, recalled at the weekly survey (p. 2), not for 'each result'. The claim could add that the authors call all estimates other than the any-change association descriptive and unadjusted (pp. 3, 5).

key_findings.correction: Precision: the 4.37 is a proportional-odds (cumulative logit) ratio, the common odds ratio of a lower amount category at either cut-point (less or none against same or more, and less, none or same against more); the Overall probabilities imply 4.20 and 4.32 (editors' calculation).
The printed values are right, but see 'missed': the benzodiazepine row's own probabilities imply an odds ratio of about 3.6 to 5.3, not 19.92.
Fig. 2 at 300 dpi: daily shares about 39% (Kentucky, around day 22) to above 80% (New York, around day 22), mostly 50% to 80%, Ohio usually highest; approximate.

reporting_issues.note: Main point confirmed (the 'fold reductions' are odds ratios; amount not measured). Correction to the description: in a proportional-odds model the odds ratio is the common ratio for a lower category at both cut-points, not only 'less or none rather than the same or more'; with the Overall probabilities the two cuts give 4.20 and 4.32. The consequence stands: less or none 9.0% against 2.3%, more 6.3% against 22.5%, so most of the absolute contrast is fewer reports of using more.
Abstract p. 1 ('OR=2.11' for 'illicit opioids or other drugs'); Results p. 6 and Table 4 p. 8 (opioids only 2.176, other 2.110, opioids and stimulants 4.207).
Table 3 lists 'I used more of the drug' and 'I used another drug along with the drug I tested' among the 12 changes; any-change probability 0.76 even after a negative result.

Table 4 footnote [1] has no matching column (p. 8, checked at 300 dpi). This matters most for the benzodiazepine row, whose intervals are very wide (using more after a negative result 0.657, 0.091 to 0.973).
Pro00068304 (p. 2) against Pro0006830 (p. 8); Fig. 1 weekly completions 454, 477, 486, 461 with losses of 16 and 45.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-I serious overall; no domain critical. Agree with each domain judgment.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the abstract's fold reductions and 'assist PWUD to immediately reduce their risks', the Discussion's 'actual reduction in amount of drugs used' (p. 6) and the Conclusions' 'compelling evidence for the impact of FTS' and 'primarily reducing the amount of fentanyl used' (p. 8), against self-reported associations in which the same amount followed 85% of positive results. The 'primarily reducing the amount of fentanyl used' wording is also at odds with Table 4, where the contrasts are smallest for illicit opioids only (OR 2.18).

missed: Internal inconsistency in Table 4 (p. 8; editors' calculation): the benzodiazepine row's modelled probabilities (positive 0.032 / 0.701 / 0.266; negative 0.009 / 0.334 / 0.657) imply odds ratios of about 3.6 (less or none against same or more) and 5.3 (less, none or same against more), not the printed 19.92 (8.57 to 46.27). The other rows reproduce approximately: overall 4.20 / 4.32 (printed 4.37), opioids only 2.18 / 2.10 (2.18), stimulants only 10.35 / 8.46 (10.04), opioids and stimulants 3.94 / 3.73 (4.21), other 2.03 / 2.01 (2.11). By the probabilities, stimulants only, not benzodiazepines, shows the largest contrast. The abstract's '20-fold' figure and the Discussion's 'strongest for those testing benzodiazepines' (p. 6) rest on the printed ratio. Claims (cl_benzo_harm_reduction_services) should not say the contrast was largest for benzodiazepines without this caveat.

The study did collect overdose (past 30 days at baseline, a covariate in every model, pp. 2-3), and the companion paper (Vickers-Smith et al., 2025, cited p. 3) reports overdoses during follow-up; this paper analyses no harm or overdose outcome. The card's 'not analysed' is right; the claim's 'measures neither harm nor overdose' is not.
Behaviour was asked for up to two strip uses a day, recalled in the weekly survey (p. 2), so 'each result' in claims should read 'up to two tests a day'.
